title: You are not testing for attrition correctly: Guest post by Jacobus Cilliers
gist: A review of 96 published field experiments finds the dominant attrition test — comparing attrition rates across treatment and control, used in 79% of studies with attrition above 1% — is neither necessary nor sufficient for unbiased estimates, and the widely used within-strata version over-rejects catastrophically: with 100 clusters and ten strata it rejects 86% of the time when nothing is wrong.

themes.theme: The standard attrition test is wrong

insights.claim: A review of 96 published field experiments with baseline data finds the most common attrition test — reported in 79 percent of experiments with attrition above 1 percent — simply checks whether attrition rates differ between treatment and control.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Four in five published experiments validate attrition with a test that does not establish what they claim, so their internal-validity assurances should be discounted.
insights.locator: The authors review 96 published field experiments

insights.claim: Equal attrition rates between arms are neither necessary for an unbiased estimate nor, without extra assumptions, sufficient: rates can differ while the estimate is fine, and identical rates can hide serious bias.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Kills the most widely cited reassurance in experimental papers; balanced attrition rates carry almost no information about bias.
insights.quote: But equal rates are neither necessary for an unbiased estimate nor, without extra assumptions, sufficient
insights.locator: The most common test

insights.claim: The second most common test, used in 61 percent of studies, checks whether treatment and control respondents are balanced at baseline — closer to correct, but only half of the correct test.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Even the better-practice studies are only running half the testable implications, so published attrition checks are systematically incomplete.
insights.quote: Closer, but only half of the correct test.
insights.locator: The second most common test

themes.theme: The two-test framework: IVal-R and IVal-P

insights.claim: Testing attrition properly requires two distinct questions: whether the treatment-control comparison is unbiased for the respondents (internal validity for respondents, IVal-R) and whether that effect also holds for the original study population (internal validity for the study population, IVal-P).
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Separates 'is the estimate valid' from 'who is it valid for' — the distinction that determines whether a result generalizes to the population you care about.
insights.locator: Ghanem and co-authors distinguish two questions

insights.claim: The respondent test's testable implication is that both columns of the treatment-by-response table are balanced at baseline jointly (treated respondents equal control respondents and treated attritors equal control attritors), while the representativeness test adds that all four cells are equal.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The joint, four-cell structure is the operational specification to demand when auditing any experimental result.
insights.locator: Test 1: Is the comparison of treatment and control respondents unbiased

insights.claim: Both tests run off one regression of the baseline outcome on treatment, an attrition indicator and their interaction with strata fixed effects: the respondent test is the joint test that the treatment and interaction coefficients are zero, and the representativeness test adds the restriction that the attrition coefficient is zero.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The correct test costs nothing extra — it runs on data researchers already have, removing any excuse for the wrong test.
insights.locator: In regression form, using the baseline outcome

insights.claim: The authors provide a Stata command that implements the full procedure, installable via `ssc install attregtest`, which reports both the within-strata and fixed-effects versions and returns one p-value per test for a whole set of variables.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Tooling availability means the corrected standard can be adopted immediately and will likely become a referee expectation.
insights.locator: The authors provide a Stata command

insights.claim: Testing balance only among respondents is wrong for two reasons: it uses only half of the testable implications of the identifying assumption, and it is often badly underpowered because program-induced responders may be 2 percent of treatment respondents yet a large proportion of the much smaller control attritor group.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Explains mechanically why respondent-only balance tests almost never reject, which is why nobody ever finds attrition problems.
insights.locator: Why also test balance among attritors?

insights.claim: The fully interacted within-strata version of the attrition test over-rejects the null badly in clustered trials: with 100 clusters even four strata is too many for the test to hold its size, and with ten strata the within-strata representativeness test rejects 86 percent of the time when nothing is wrong.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Published studies using the within-strata version may have flagged or been criticized for attrition problems that do not exist.
insights.quote: with ten strata the within-strata representativeness test rejects 86 percent of the time when nothing is wrong
insights.locator: 1. The fully interacted version over-rejects the null

insights.claim: The same over-rejection problem arises with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors under individual-level randomization but is far less severe there, only starting to bite once strata fall below roughly 200 observations each.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Clustered designs are where the diagnostic breaks down; individual-level trials are relatively safe above 200 observations per stratum.
insights.locator: The same problem arises with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors

insights.claim: The fully interacted test also has lower power because of its many degrees of freedom, and family-wise error rate corrections are conservative, which hands researchers a way to falsely conclude that attrition is not a problem.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Notes a perverse incentive: the least reliable test is also the one most likely to deliver the comfortable answer researchers want.
insights.quote: That hands researchers a way to falsely conclude that attrition is not a problem.
insights.locator: 2. Lower statistical power

insights.claim: Which test has most power depends on the nature of attrition: when bias is diffuse across strata the fixed-effects test has the most power and the per-stratum approach with FWER correction the least, and the ranking flips when the violation is concentrated in a single stratum.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Test choice must be pre-specified because it is outcome-dependent, otherwise it becomes a researcher degree of freedom.
insights.locator: A second set of simulations

insights.claim: The practical recommendation is to use the strata fixed-effects version, which the paper's authors themselves propose for this situation and use in their own empirical exercise whenever there are more than ten strata; the trade-off is that it tests an implication of the sharp restriction rather than the restriction itself.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A clear default for practitioners, with the cost of the default stated explicitly.
insights.locator: So I believe it is more sensible to just use the fixed-effects test

insights.claim: Attrition tests should be run separately for each endline outcome using that outcome's own baseline value and its own response indicator, with a multiple-testing correction across outcomes, because attrition rates can vary by outcome within the same survey.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A single study can be representative for one outcome and not another, so per-outcome validity claims are required.
insights.locator: What about multiple outcomes?

insights.claim: Progresa illustrates why per-outcome testing matters: school enrollment fails the representativeness test while adult employment passes it, even though both come from the same survey, because households with more school-age children were more likely to skip the enrollment questions.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A worked case where outcome-specific non-response silently biases exactly the outcome the program targets.
insights.locator: The paper uses Progresa to show why the per-outcome approach matters

insights.claim: Where baseline data for an outcome are missing, only specific covariates are admissible for testing — determinants of the outcome, or proxies driven by the same unobservables as the outcome — and these should be pre-specified as a small set and tested jointly with the baseline outcome where available.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Restricts a common escape hatch where researchers test whatever covariates happen to be balanced.
insights.locator: What if you lack baseline data for an outcome?

insights.claim: With k variables the respondent test stacks 2k restrictions and the representativeness test 3k, and in simulations with 100 clusters a representativeness test over ten variables at once falsely rejects 37 percent of the time, so with more than two or three variables in a clustered design another approach is needed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Gives a hard rule of thumb — more than two or three variables in a clustered design breaks the joint test.
insights.locator: The same warning as above applies

insights.claim: The most viable alternative for many variables in a clustered design is testing each variable separately with a family-wise error rate or false discovery rate adjustment such as Anderson's (2008) sharpened q-values, which in simulations falsely rejects roughly 7 to 8 percent of the time for a 5 percent test.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A slightly oversized but usable fallback, with its size distortion quantified rather than assumed away.
insights.locator: The most viable alternative is to test each variable separately

insights.claim: Randomization inference is not strictly justified for attrition testing under cluster-level assignment because attrition is itself a post-treatment outcome — reshuffling schools into treatment and control shuffles their response rates too — and in simulations its power is lower than adjusting for multiple tests with Anderson q-values.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Closes off the intuitive alternative fix, narrowing the defensible method set.
insights.locator: (Aside: my first instinct was to use randomization inference

themes.theme: A worked example and the bottom line

insights.claim: In a long-run follow-up of the Early Grade Reading Study in South Africa, 67 percent of the treatment group (655 of 981 learners) and 66 percent of the control group (1,035 of 1,575) were found and assessed — high attrition but similar across arms.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The textbook case where the standard rate-comparison test would have declared no problem.
insights.locator: An example from my own work

insights.claim: In that study the respondent test never rejects while the representativeness test rejects for every variable and jointly: the lost learners are about a third of a year older, 10 percentage points less likely to be girls, and 0.2 standard deviations weaker on the baseline learning index, equally in both arms — so the estimates speak only for the two-thirds of the sample that could be found.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Shows the practical payoff: the estimate survives as internally valid but its population of reference shrinks materially.
insights.locator: But the representativeness (IVal-P) test rejects for every variable

insights.claim: The within-strata version of the same test rejects the respondent test for the learning index (p = 0.004) and for all three variables jointly (p < 0.001), which would have wrongly implied the study was not internally valid even for respondents — with ten strata and 130 schools it stacks 60 restrictions on 130 clusters.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A concrete demonstration that the wrong version of the test manufactures fatal-looking results from nothing.
insights.locator: BUT. The within-strata version of the test

insights.claim: The recommended practice is to report attrition rates by arm with cell sizes as a description of the response process rather than a validity test, report the four cell means and two joint p-values per outcome from one regression, and pre-specify both the variables and, if stratified, the test version.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A ready-made reporting standard that referees and evidence consumers can apply immediately.
insights.locator: The bottom line

insights.claim: If the representativeness test fails, researchers should state plainly which population the estimate covers; if the respondent test fails, no test will rescue the study and it moves into the territory of attrition corrections and bounds.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A decision rule for how much weight to put on a study once its attrition diagnostics are known.
insights.quote: If the respondent test fails, no test will rescue you: you are in the territory of attrition corrections and bounds.
insights.locator: The bottom line
